name: The Resurrection and the Final Judgment
path: Eschatology: The Doctrine of Last Things

objectives.text: Identify from Scripture that God will raise the dead to life on the last day
Recall that Jesus will come to judge the living and the dead, as Scripture and the Apostles' Creed state
Retell the account of Jesus rising bodily from the dead and state that it shows God's power to raise his people
Explain that the same body that dies will be raised, changed in its qualities but not replaced by a different body
Identify from Scripture that every person, great and small, will stand before Christ to give an account
Describe the contrasts Paul draws between the present body and the resurrection body of believers
Explain what Scripture teaches will happen to believers who are still alive on the last day
Compare the resurrection of the just to honor with the resurrection of the unjust to dishonor
Explain from Scripture that the final judgment will bring every thought, word, and deed into account
Explain why the Father has appointed Christ as judge and how Paul presents Christ's resurrection as proof of the coming judgment
Explain how Paul uses the coming resurrection to instruct believers about grieving and about steadfast labor in the Lord
Analyze the final judgment in terms of its judge, its subjects, and its standard
Trace the hope of bodily resurrection through Old Testament passages and explain how the New Testament develops it
Interpret the separation of the sheep and the goats in its context, explaining how works serve as evidence rather than the ground of acceptance
Analyze Paul's firstfruits argument connecting Christ's resurrection, by the Spirit, to the resurrection of believers
Explain the purpose of the last judgment as the Reformed tradition confesses it, the display of God's mercy and justice
Explain how the Reformed tradition relates justification by faith to judgment according to works, including the open acquittal of believers
Explain the reasons the Westminster Confession gives for the certainty of the judgment and the hiddenness of its day
Analyze Paul's argument about the consequences for the gospel if there is no resurrection of the dead
Compare how the Westminster Standards, the Belgic Confession, and the Heidelberg Catechism state the doctrines of resurrection and judgment
Evaluate views that deny a bodily resurrection or a final judgment, from the Sadducees and early spiritualizing errors to modern universalism, using Scripture
Defend the justice of God in the final judgment against common objections using Scripture
Compose a theological essay that synthesizes resurrection and judgment as the vindication of God and his people, drawing on Scripture and the confessions

changes: Kept and reworded the real competencies: raising the dead, the day of judgment, bodily resurrection, the resurrection of just and unjust, the resurrection body, judge, subjects, and standard, sheep and goats, firstfruits, purpose of judgment, evaluating denials, defending God's justice, and the capstone synthesis. Recast the grief objective as explaining Paul's instruction so it no longer targets feelings. Merged 'observe everyone will stand before God' into an objective with clear anchors. Replaced the vague 'construct a theology' with a confessional comparison and a capstone essay. Added missing competencies: identity of the raised body, change of the living, judgment of thoughts, words, and deeds, Christ appointed as judge, the Old Testament resurrection hope, justification and judgment according to works, WCF 33.3 on the certainty of judgment and its hidden day, and Paul's 1 Corinthians 15 argument. Left Christ's return, the intermediate state, the new creation, hell, and millennial views to the sibling sub-topics. Corrected confession citations to full document names and added the Heidelberg Catechism and Belgic Confession where they state the doctrine.
